title: Building a Column That Makes Index Into Position
concept_layer: array as indexed memory; index = distance; for-loop as space-walk
domain_deferred: hash maps and associative indexing → graphtheory / DataStructures
2D and 3D grids → later in arrays sequence (grid_2d_4x4, grid_3d_4x4x4)

capture_leaks.contiguity: This array looks continuous — the cubes touch. But an array is logically a sequence of addressable slots; 'next to' is a property of the rendering, not of the index.
capture_leaks.fixed_size: range(4) is hardcoded. Dynamic-size arrays, resizing costs, and memory layout are deferred to later sequences.
capture_leaks.flat_addressing: A 1D array can represent a 2D grid via i = row*width + col. This encoding trick is invisible here; grid_2d_4x4 makes it explicit.
capture_leaks.linear_traversal: for-loop walks 0→1→2→3. But arrays also support binary search, hash lookup, jumps — the linearity of the loop is a convention, not the only path.
capture_leaks.homogeneous_cells: Every cube is identical. Heterogeneous arrays (different types per index) require more machinery — structs, tuples, tagged unions.

limit: Four cubes in a line. A ruler made of objects. What it captures beautifully: that an index IS a position, that a for-loop IS a walk, that [0] and [1] are not abstractions but places you can stand next to. What it refuses: dynamic resizing, non-linear access, associative keys, variable types per cell. Later maps take those up; this one makes countable space touchable.

grammar_alignment.note: column_3_z teaches only `repeat` — the simplest operation. The other three arrays operations are taught by sibling artifacts later in the sequence.

biome_alignment.note: The biome now has first vegetation AND gridagents roaming. Array concepts unlock the verbs 'snap_place' (put a thing at an index) and 'reorder' (rearrange indices). The world is still mostly sterile but beginning to populate — density 0.2.

stages.title: From force to formation
stages.thinking: ForcesFoundations taught that F = m·a is the same equation for falling apples and orbiting planets. Forces accumulate into motion. Now a question that forces can't answer: if I want four objects in a row, how do I say 'four' to code? Not how they move — how they are organized. The answer is the array. Position was one Vector3. An array is many of them, addressed by index.
stages.code:
# Previous sequences:
#   primitives — one thing at a time (Vector3, line, triangle)
#   transformation — how to move one thing
#   color — how one thing looks
#   forces — how one thing reacts
#
# Now: many things, addressed by number.
#
# position = Vector3(0, 0, 0)    # one location
# positions = [Vector3(0,0,0), Vector3(0,0,1), ...]
# positions[0]   → the first one
# positions[i]   → the i-th one
#
# Index is a new kind of parameter.
# Not spatial, not temporal — ORDINAL.

stages.title: The for-loop as a walk
stages.thinking: GDScript's for-loop is the primary tool for creating an array. `for i in range(4)` runs the body four times, with i taking values 0, 1, 2, 3 in order. This is not 'iteration' as an abstraction — it is a walk. The map will literally be a walk alongside four cubes, so the loop that creates them is a walk in code. Structure mirrors experience.

stages.title: Index becomes distance
stages.thinking: Here is the move that makes the whole map work: i * 1.0 along the Z axis. The mathematical abstraction (i is an index) becomes a physical fact (i is a distance in meters). Cube[0] sits at z=0. Cube[1] sits at z=1. The player can walk from [0] to [1] and feel that distance IS the step from one index to the next. Indexing is no longer abstract.
stages.code:
for i in range(4):
	var cube_instance = pickup_cube_scene.instantiate()
	cube_instance.name = "Cube_" + str(i)
	
	# Position cubes `spacing` units apart in Z direction
	# index becomes distance
	cube_instance.position = Vector3(0, 0, i * 1.0)
	
	add_child(cube_instance)

# When the player walks from z=0 to z=3,
# they are walking the array from [0] to [3].
# The body learns what index means.

stages.title: Label each slot with its index
stages.thinking: Without labels, four cubes is just four cubes. With [0] [1] [2] [3] floating above them, the cubes become an array. Label3D with billboard mode ensures the label faces the player from any angle. Pink is the color — specifically Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.8). In Ada Research, pink codes 'soft' rather than 'rigid.' An array is a structure, but the structure is not hard; it's a convention the world agrees to.
stages.code:
var label = Label3D.new()
label.text = "[%d]" % i
label.font_size = 24
label.pixel_size = 0.003
label.outline_size = 0
label.position = Vector3(0, 1.0, 0)  # floats above cube
label.billboard = BaseMaterial3D.BILLBOARD_ENABLED
label.modulate = Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.8)  # soft pink
cube_instance.add_child(label)

# [0] is not a number above a cube.
# It is the NAME of that cube.
# The cube BECOMES its index.

stages.title: Pick up = remove from array
stages.thinking: The cubes are pickable. When the player grabs one and walks away with it, what happens? The array has a hole. The slot remains (no cube-shift to fill it). This is array semantics: indices are addresses, not ranks. Remove index 2, and the array still has [0], [1], null, [3]. This is the first implicit lesson about associative vs sequential thinking.
stages.code:
# pickup_cube.tscn is an XRToolsPickable
# When picked, the cube leaves its parent hierarchy
# in practice — it's carried by the player's hand.
# The column_3_z remains, but [2] is visibly missing.
#
# This is NOT:
#   cubes.remove(2)   # would shift [3] into slot 2
# 
# This IS:
#   cubes[2] = null   # slot stays, content gone
#
# Later sequences will teach:
#   - shifting (linked lists) → data structures
#   - resizing (dynamic arrays) → procgen
#   - associative arrays (hash maps) → graph theory

stages.title: Parameterize via apply_grid_config
stages.thinking: The artifact accepts configuration at placement time: count (how many cubes), spacing (how far apart), label_size, label_color. This pattern — apply_grid_config(config: Dictionary) — is project-wide. Any artifact can be parameterized by the map that places it. Same artifact, different parameters, different lessons. column_3_z:count=8:spacing=0.5 teaches density; count=2:spacing=3.0 teaches sparsity.

stages.title: Clean up cubes that weren't auto-parented
stages.thinking: A small but telling detail. `for child in get_children(): if not child.owner: child.queue_free()`. When an artifact dies (exits tree or is rebuilt), any children without an owner — i.e., ones we created procedurally in code — need to be freed explicitly. Children with an owner came from a .tscn scene and get cleaned up automatically. This distinction shows up everywhere in procedural Godot code.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: An array column knows what it is. Not four cubes — an ordered sequence of addresses made spatial. The soft pink label color is not decoration; it is the project's signal that structure is not the enemy of softness. The spacing parameter is not adjustable just for layout; it is the critical parameter because it controls whether the array feels continuous (spacing=1, cubes touch) or separate (spacing>1, gaps visible). When you walk from [0] to [3], you are doing what a for-loop does. You are the iteration.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: for i in range(4): cube.position = Vector3(0, 0, i × spacing) — four pickup cubes arranged as a linear array in the Z direction, each labeled [i]
# desire: to walk alongside an array — to see [0], [1], [2], [3] as physical objects in space and understand that an index is a distance, that traversal is movement
# critical_parameter: spacing — at 1.0 the cubes are adjacent and the array feels compact; at 2.0 they feel like separate objects; the default 1.0 makes index=position visible
# triggers: picking up a cube removes it from the array visualization, making the gap visible — the array has a hole where the index used to be
# emerges: the pink label color (Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.8)) subtly codes the array as soft rather than rigid, echoing the project's queer aesthetic
# needs: pickup cubes [has]; Label3D index labels [has]; apply_grid_config supports count/spacing/label overrides [has]
# relationships: simpler than grid_2d_4x4 (one dimension vs two); appears in Tutorial_Row alongside xyz_coordinates; precedes grid_2d_4x4
# truth: an array is space made countable — column_3_z makes the abstract concept of an index into a physical position you can walk to
